How Much Life Does an Extra Dollar Buy? The Health-Income Curve in 154 Countries

economics
data visualization
R
Published

October 26, 2026

Code 
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(plotly)

# All data come from the analysis repository
base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog7-health-income/main/"

panel    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "data/processed/panel.csv"))
by_year  <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/preston_by_year.csv"))
shift    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/curve_shift.csv"))
covid    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/covid_by_income.csv"))
outliers <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/outliers.csv"))
key      <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/key_stats.csv"))
sens     <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/sensitivity.csv"))

# Helpers for inline numbers
ks  <- function(stat) key$value[key$stat == stat]
num <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
grp <- function(g, col) covid[[col]][covid$income_group == g]

# One row per World Bank region: raw name, short label, colour
region_table <- tibble(
  region = c("East Asia & Pacific", "Europe & Central Asia",
             "Latin America & Caribbean",
             "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan",
             "North America", "South Asia", "Sub-Saharan Africa"),
  region_short = c("East Asia & Pacific", "Europe & Central Asia",
                   "Latin America & Caribbean", "Middle East & North Africa",
                   "North America", "South Asia", "Sub-Saharan Africa"),
  color = c("#2b8cbe", "#7b3294", "#e6550d", "#a6761d",
            "#31a354", "#756bb1", "#c51b8a")
)
region_colors <- setNames(region_table$color, region_table$region_short)

The question

Every government publishes a GDP per capita number and a life expectancy number, but the two are almost never read against each other across countries. Read together, they produce a price. The Preston curve plots life expectancy against log GDP per capita for all countries in a given year, and its slope answers a plain question: if a country’s income doubles, how many more years of life does it buy?

Two things make the curve worth watching over time. First, the slope has been strikingly stable: about 4.7 years of life per doubling of income for three decades. Stability turns the curve into a measuring instrument, because if the price of income is roughly constant, then any movement of the whole curve is a change in the technology of survival — medicine, sanitation, nutrition, vaccination — that income does not capture. Second, the curve has been moving, and it has been moving faster at the bottom of the income distribution than at the top.

Data and method

The data come from the World Bank Indicators API (CC BY 4.0), three indicators for every country from 1990 to 2023: life expectancy at birth (SP.DYN.LE00.IN), GDP per capita at PPP in constant 2021 international dollars (NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD), and population (SP.POP.TOTL). The panel keeps 154 countries over 1990–2023 (5,081 country-years) after dropping World Bank aggregates, country-years missing any indicator, and countries with fewer than one million inhabitants, whose life expectancy is estimated from small numbers and swings wildly between years.

The method is deliberately simple. Life expectancy is regressed on log2(GDP per capita) separately in each year; the slope is the price of income. The fitted curve is then read off at $5,000 and $40,000 to measure how it moved over time. For the pandemic, each country’s actual 2019–2021 change is compared with its own 2010–2019 pace, annualised and projected across the two pandemic years, so that the comparison is not contaminated by the two windows having different lengths.

1. What an extra dollar buys

Fitting the curve year by year gives a median slope of 4.67 years of life per doubling of income, and 4.63 in a pooled model with year effects. The fit is good — R² runs from 0.68 in 1990 to 0.78 in 2023 — so income explains most, but far from all, of the cross-country spread in life expectancy.

The residual is the interesting part. Around the line sit countries that reach far more, or far less, life expectancy than their income predicts: not necessarily rich or poor countries, but countries whose health outcomes are out of line with their material circumstances.

2. The curve moved up, and moved up more for the poor

Reading the fitted curve at two reference incomes shows how much the whole relationship shifted between 1990 and 2019.

Code 
shift |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2005, 2019, 2021, 2023)) |>
  transmute(
    Year = year,
    `At $5,000`  = sprintf("%+.2f", shift_5k_vs_1990),
    `At $40,000` = sprintf("%+.2f", shift_40k_vs_1990)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
Year At $5,000 At $40,000
1990 +0.00 +0.00
2005 +2.31 +1.64
2019 +5.09 +3.47
2021 +4.19 +1.71
2023 +6.45 +3.31

A country at $5,000 per capita in 2019 would have been expected to live about 5.09 years less than the 1990 curve predicted for that income; at $40,000 the gap is 3.47 years. The curve did not shift up uniformly. It shifted up more at the bottom, which is the signature of improvements that matter most where health starts from a low base: the disease environment improved for everyone, and poorer countries had more to gain from it.

3. The interactive view: the curve, one year at a time

A static scatter plot of the 2019 cross-section answers one question — where do countries sit relative to income this year — and answers it well. It is close to useless for the question I actually care about, which is how the relationship moves. So the main figure below is an interactive one: the cross-section is animated from 1990 to 2023, with the fitted curve re-drawn for every year.

Code 
hover_text <- panel |>
  left_join(region_table, by = "region") |>
  mutate(
    marker_size = 4 + 36 * sqrt(population / max(population)),
    label = paste0("<b>", country_name, "</b><br>",
                   "Year: ", year, "<br>",
                   "Life expectancy: ", round(life_expectancy, 1), " years<br>",
                   "GDP per capita: $", format(round(gdp_per_capita), big.mark = ","), "<br>",
                   "Population: ", format(round(population / 1e6), big.mark = ","), " million<br>",
                   "Region: ", region_short, "<br>",
                   "Income group: ", income_group)
  )

curve_all <- by_year |>
  filter(!is.na(slope)) |>
  select(year, intercept, slope) |>
  crossing(gdp_per_capita = exp(seq(log(1500), log(150000), length.out = 100))) |>
  mutate(predicted = intercept + slope * log2(gdp_per_capita))

plot_ly(
  data = hover_text,
  x = ~gdp_per_capita, y = ~life_expectancy,
  color = ~region_short, frame = ~year,
  text = ~label, hoverinfo = "text",
  type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
  marker = list(size = hover_text$marker_size, opacity = 0.65, sizemin = 3,
                line = list(width = 0.4, color = "white")),
  colors = region_colors
) |>
  add_trace(
    data = curve_all, x = ~gdp_per_capita, y = ~predicted, frame = ~year,
    inherit = FALSE,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = "black", width = 1.4, dash = "dot"),
    hoverinfo = "none", showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "", type = "log", range = c(log10(1500), log10(150000)),
                 tickvals = c(2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000),
                 ticktext = c("$2k", "$5k", "$10k", "$20k", "$50k", "$100k")),
    yaxis = list(title = "Life expectancy at birth (years)", range = c(38, 90)),
    title = list(
      text = "The health-income curve, one year at a time<br><sup>Drag the slider or press play to step through 1990–2023</sup>",
      font = list(size = 16)
    ),
    annotations = list(
      list(x = 0, y = -0.035, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
           xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
           text = "GDP per capita (PPP, 2021 international dollars, log scale)",
           font = list(size = 11, color = "#444444"))
    ),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Region"), orientation = "v",
                  x = 1.02, xanchor = "left", y = 1, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(l = 95, r = 150, t = 80, b = 130),
    hoverlabel = list(bgcolor = "white")
  ) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 700, transition = 300) |>
  config(displaylogo = FALSE, responsive = TRUE, scrollZoom = TRUE)

Three interactions earn their place here. The animation makes the upward movement of the curve a thing you watch rather than a number you are told. The legend switches regions on and off, which separates the question “how does income relate to life expectancy” from “is the Sub-Saharan African cluster tight or is it scattered”, and the answer is visibly not tight. The hover tooltips name every country and report its life expectancy, GDP per capita, population, region and income group, so any point in the cloud can be identified and checked. Bubble area is proportional to population, so the reader can see that the countries that matter for most of the world’s people are not the ones sitting furthest from the line.

4. The pandemic interrupted the pattern

Between 2019 and 2021 life expectancy fell in almost every country in the world, and the interruption was not spread evenly across income levels. Comparing what happened against each country’s own pre-pandemic pace isolates the break.

Code 
covid |>
  mutate(income_group = factor(income_group,
                               levels = c("Low", "Lower-middle", "Upper-middle", "High"))) |>
  arrange(income_group) |>
  transmute(
    `Income group` = income_group,
    n = n,
    `2010–2019 (yr/yr)` = sprintf("%+.2f", med_pre_pace),
    `2019–2021 (yr/yr)` = sprintf("%+.2f", med_covid_pace),
    `Behind trend` = sprintf("%.2f years", med_excess)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrcrr")
Income group n 2010–2019 (yr/yr) 2019–2021 (yr/yr) Behind trend
Low 21 +0.43 -0.10 -1.19 years
Lower-middle 39 +0.32 -0.45 -1.57 years
Upper-middle 43 +0.23 -1.22 -2.95 years
High 50 +0.20 -0.53 -1.52 years

Life expectancy was rising in every income group before the pandemic and fell in every income group during it. The upper-middle group lost the most — 2.95 years against its own trend — and the loss is concentrated: Paraguay, South Africa, Botswana, Peru, Ecuador and Mexico each lost four to six years. High-income countries lost least, and the ones that lost almost nothing are the ones with the lowest COVID mortality and the slowest pre-pandemic pace: Australia, New Zealand, Norway, Japan.

The comparison uses medians rather than means on purpose. In a group of 21 low-income countries, one country in a mortality crisis — the Central African Republic — moves the mean a long way, and it moves it in the wrong direction: the mean low-income loss would read 0.65 years instead of 1.19.

5. Who is above and below the curve

Residuals are taken from a pooled regression with year fixed effects, so each country is compared with what other countries were achieving in the same year rather than with a global average that ignores the curve’s own movement. The twelve largest positive and negative residuals over 1990–2023 are in results/outliers.csv; the largest gaps are Albania (8.94 years), West Bank and Gaza (8.44 years) and China (8.38 years) on one side, and Nigeria (15.65 years), Eswatini (15.55 years) and Equatorial Guinea on the other. Every one of the twelve countries below the curve is in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Income is not the same thing as health. A country can be healthy for reasons that are not in its income — a strong public health system, a diet, a low violence rate — and that is visible in the residuals, which are large, stable over three decades, and concentrated in a handful of countries with recognizable stories behind them.

6. Spotlighting a single country

The animation answers “how did the curve move”. The figure below answers the complementary question: how did individual countries move? Every country is drawn as a thin grey line that can be hovered, the seven regional medians are highlighted and can be switched on and off in the legend, and the menu spotlights one country against the backdrop of all the others. Switch it to China or Nigeria and the difference in starting point, slope and pandemic dip is immediate in a way that no table conveys.

Code 
all_lines <- panel |>
  arrange(country_iso3, year) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("<b>", country_name, "</b><br>Year: ", year,
                        "<br>Life expectancy: ", round(life_expectancy, 1), " years"))

regional_medians <- panel |>
  left_join(region_table, by = "region") |>
  group_by(region, region_short, year) |>
  summarise(median_life = median(life_expectancy), .groups = "drop")

# The menu offers the countries the analysis flagged as interesting, plus a
# spread of large economies, so it stays usable.
spotlight <- sort(unique(c(
  outliers$country_name,
  c("China", "India", "United States", "Brazil", "Nigeria", "Japan", "Germany",
    "Russia", "Indonesia", "Mexico", "Bangladesh", "Ethiopia")
)))
spotlight <- spotlight[spotlight %in% panel$country_name]

n_regions    <- nrow(region_table)
n_countries  <- length(spotlight)
total_traces <- 1 + n_regions + n_countries

# The dropdown is built from a visibility vector over the traces:
# 1 = all countries, 2..(1+n_regions) = the regional medians, the rest = one
# trace per spotlit country.
make_visible <- function(country) {
  vis <- rep("legendonly", total_traces)
  vis[1] <- "true"
  vis[2:(1 + n_regions)] <- "true"
  vis[1 + n_regions + match(country, spotlight)] <- "true"
  vis
}

p5 <- plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data = all_lines, x = ~year, y = ~life_expectancy, text = ~label, hoverinfo = "text",
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = "#c9c9c9", width = 0.6),
    showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE
  )

for (i in seq_len(n_regions)) {
  p5 <- p5 |>
    add_trace(
      data = regional_medians |> filter(region == region_table$region[i]),
      x = ~year, y = ~median_life, name = region_table$region_short[i],
      type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
      line = list(width = 2.6, color = region_table$color[i]),
      hoverinfo = "y", inherit = FALSE
    )
}

for (cc in spotlight) {
  p5 <- p5 |>
    add_trace(
      data = panel |> filter(country_name == cc),
      x = ~year, y = ~life_expectancy,
      name = cc, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
      line = list(color = "#d6336c", width = 2.2),
      hoverinfo = "x+y", showlegend = FALSE,
      visible = if (cc == spotlight[1]) "true" else "legendonly",
      inherit = FALSE
    )
}

p5 |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Year", dtick = 5),
    yaxis = list(title = "Life expectancy at birth (years)", range = c(35, 90)),
    annotations = list(
      list(x = 0, y = 1.20, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
           showarrow = FALSE, text = "<b>Life expectancy trajectories, 1990–2023</b>",
           font = list(size = 16)),
      list(x = 0, y = 1.13, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
           showarrow = FALSE, align = "left",
           text = "Every country is a thin grey line. Use the menu to spotlight one of them.",
           font = list(size = 11, color = "#666666"))
    ),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Regional median"), orientation = "v",
                  x = 1.02, xanchor = "left", y = 1, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(l = 70, r = 190, t = 150, b = 60),
    updatemenus = list(list(
      type = "dropdown", direction = "down", x = 0, y = 1.06, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
      active = 0,
      buttons = lapply(spotlight, function(cc) {
        list(label = cc, method = "restyle", args = list(list(visible = make_visible(cc))))
      })
    ))
  ) |>
  config(displaylogo = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)

Robustness

Seven of the 5,081 country-year observations are acute mortality crises rather than informative points on the income–health relation: Rwanda in 1994 (12.2 years of life), Somalia in 1991–93, and the Central African Republic in 2009, 2019 and 2022. They are genuine observations and they stay in the main analysis, but the headline numbers were re-estimated without them. The median slope moves from 4.67 to 4.61, the shift at $5,000 from 5.09 to 5.58 years, and the pandemic losses are unchanged to two decimals. The conclusions do not depend on the crisis years.

Limitations

  • The curve is cross-sectional. It describes what countries at a given income achieve, not what happens to a country when its income changes, so it is not a causal return on income.
  • Life expectancy is a population average. It says nothing about inequality within a country.
  • Income groups are the current classification applied to all years, so a country that moved between groups is counted in its present group throughout.
  • The pandemic window is short. Some of the 2021 “excess loss” is catch-up rather than permanent loss, and a longer window would spread the same total over more years.

Takeaway

Income buys life, and the price has been remarkably stable: about 4.67 years per doubling, every year, for thirty years. The interesting part is what happens around that price. The curve has been drifting upward underneath it — faster at the bottom, so a poor country gained about 5.09 years between 1990 and 2019 where a rich one gained 3.47 — which is what it looks like when public health technology improves faster than income grows. And then the pandemic took it all back for two years, everywhere, with the middle-income countries losing the most against their own trend.

None of this says that income stops mattering. The slope is still about 4.7 years per doubling. What the analysis adds is the size of the residuals: some countries live many years more, and some many years less, than their income predicts. Income is the price of health, but it is not the whole bill.

Code and data: github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog7-health-income. Data source: World Bank Indicators (CC BY 4.0).
